content: The study investigated whether body positioning could be an effective, non-invasive method to reduce clinically significant apnoea in preterm infants who breathe spontaneously. The primary objective was to evaluate the effects of different body positions on cardiorespiratory parameters, such as apnoea, bradycardia, and oxygen saturation, in this population. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the impact of body positioning in specific groups of preterm infants, including those with a gestational age of less than 28 weeks or a birth weight below 1000 grams, those whose apnoea was managed with methylxanthines, those experiencing frequent apnoea (more than 10 events per day), and those with different types of apnoea (central, mixed, or obstructive). The researchers employed the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group to identify relevant studies. They searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), covering publications up to November 14, 2016. Additionally, clinical trial registries and conference proceedings were reviewed to identify randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomised trials that compared the effects of various body positions on apnoea in spontaneously breathing preterm infants. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials with parallel, factorial, or cross-over designs that assessed the impact of body positioning on apnoea in preterm infants. The quality of the included trials was evaluated, and data were extracted and synthesised using standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was used to assess the quality of the evidence. The search conducted in November 2016 did not identify any new studies. A total of five studies, involving 114 preterm infants, met the inclusion criteria. However, none of the individual studies or meta-analyses demonstrated a significant reduction in apnoea, bradycardia, oxygen desaturation, or oxygen saturation with any specific body position. The positions compared included supine versus prone, prone versus right lateral, prone versus left lateral, right lateral versus left lateral, prone horizontal versus prone with head elevation, right lateral horizontal versus right lateral with head elevation, and left lateral horizontal versus left lateral with head elevation. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effects of body positioning on apnoea, bradycardia, and oxygen saturation in spontaneously breathing preterm infants. No new studies have been conducted since the original review was published. The authors recommend that large, multi-centre studies are needed to provide conclusive evidence. However, based on the available data, it may be reasonable to infer that body positioning does not significantly influence the cardiorespiratory parameters of spontaneously breathing preterm infants.
